overview.text: Apocalypse, as an eschatological idea, concerns the anticipated end or transformation of the world or of its present order. Eschatology also includes beliefs about individual destinies, but this topic focuses on cosmic endings. Traditions differ: an ending may involve judgment and the defeat of evil, yet also renewal or a new age, rather than simple annihilation. The word “apocalypse” originally meant an unveiling or revelation; it is also used for visionary writings about divine realities and events at the end of time. For example, Christian Revelation uses vivid symbolic visions, while Zoroastrian teaching describes frashokereti, a final renovation of creation. These are religious teachings, not verified predictions.

key_facts.text: Eschatology can address both an individual’s fate after death and the future of the world; cosmic eschatology is the world-focused branch.
“Apocalypse” comes from a Greek word for revelation or unveiling; in ancient Jewish and Christian writing, it can refer to a visionary literary form.
In the Christian Book of Revelation, apocalyptic imagery includes visions arranged around seven seals, trumpets, and bowls.
In Zoroastrian teaching, frashokereti names a final renovation in which evil is overcome, the dead rise, and creation is renewed.
Zoroastrian accounts developed over time, and later texts vary in some details; early and later accounts should not be treated as identical.
